To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the splitting criteria and the pruning methods of decision trees are influenced in different ways by the misclassification cost and the class distribution.

(1) the splitting criteria of the decision tree learning algorithms we investigated were relatively insensitive to costs, and (2) pruning methods that were cost sensitive performed well in terms of expected cost, and that pruning methods that were insensitive to costs performed poorly.

the splitting criteria that are relatively less sensitive to costs or prior class distributions perform as well as, and sometimes even better than, splitting criteria that have been explicitly designed to be cost sensitive.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: how does a change in the class distribution (or misclassification costs) affect a decision tree algorithm?
the question: "Can decision trees be made cost-sensitive without changing the splitting criterion?"
how to build a decision tree that is robust with respect to misclassification costs or class distributions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cost-sensitive decision trees are no better than cost-insensitive trees.
, in terms of the expected misclassification cost of the final decision tree, there is no significant benefit in using any of the cost-sensitive splitting criteria.
, if the cost is not known or is not known well, it is better to use a cost-insensitive algorithm, but, if the cost can be known, it is better, in general, to use a cost-sensitive algorithm.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the best decision tree algorithms are those that are cost-insensitive.
the cost-insensitive splitting criterion and pruning method combination is a good choice for dealing with imbalance.
, for a decision tree learning algorithm, the splitting criterion and pruning method should be considered as two independent factors and that the splitting criterion should be chosen first.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cost insensitivity of the splitting criterion is a key factor in determining whether a decision tree algorithm is cost sensitive.
the cost (in)sensitivity of decision tree algorithms should not be taken for granted.
the splitting criterion should be chosen to minimize the effect of the class distribution and misclassification cost on the decision tree.
